KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and very humid conditions are expected to 
persist through Tuesday of next week. A Heat Advisory is in 
effect for portions of the area.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern is developing across our
region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be in place
through the middle of next week as Bermuda high pressure
persists offshore. This will keep a steady stream of very warm
and moist air in place across the region through the period.

A prolonged period of hot and, most notably, very humid 
conditions is expected to remain in place for the next several 
days. We look to have a weak cold frontal passage early Sunday,
ushering in slightly drier air. This will give some slight 
reprieve from the excessive humidity, though highs will still 
be in the upper 80s to low 90s. Moisture advection will return 
again by Monday though, and hot and very humid conditions are 
anticipated to return Monday through Tuesday. A somewhat 
stronger cold front looks to come through late Tuesday or 
Wednesday, which will help break the excessive heat and humidity
some.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect for portions of eastern 
Pennsylvania, much of New Jersey except the far southern 
counties, as well as New Castle, Delware. The Heat Advisory was
expanded to include coastal Monmouth County, as southwesterly
surface winds should prevent the sea breeze from making much
inland progress there. The end time of the Heat Advisory for 
Carbon and Monroe Counties was changed to end at 8 PM this 
evening, as the forecast for Friday has trended well below 
advisory criteria. The Heat Advisory for the I-95 corridor and 
portions of central and southern New Jersey was extended through
8 PM Saturday, where confidence is highest in heat indices 
reaching near or over 100 degrees on Saturday. Elsewhere in 
eastern Pennsylvania and northern New Jersey, the Heat Advisory 
remains in effect through 8 PM Friday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...There are daily chances for showers and 
thunderstorms through Saturday, as well as much of next week. 
There is at least a marginal risk each day for localized heavy 
rainfall leading to flash flooding and locally damaging wind 
gusts with any stronger thunderstorms that develop.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern is developing across our
region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be in place
through the middle of next week as Bermuda high pressure
persists offshore. This will keep a steady stream of very warm
and moist air in place across the region through the period,
with varying kinematics and forcing aloft. Mid level flow does
appear to increase by early next week, which may be more
supportive of better organized and stronger convection compared
to this week.

Diurnally driven instability will be in the 1000-2000 J/kg each
afternoon through the next several days along with PWats in the
1.5-2" range. Mean flow will be predominantly southwesterly and
relatively weak through Saturday. This will support a continued
localized heavy rainfall threat with potential for flash 
flooding, although water loaded downdrafts could cause localized
wind damage. Areas with very saturated ground from recent rains
will be most prone to experiencing trees falling.

Convection today should be confined primarily northwest of the
I-95 corridor where forcing aloft is most supportive, though 
cannot rule our some storms making it as far southeast as the 
I-95 corridor. SPC and WPC maintain a Marginal Risks in this 
area. On Friday, convection looks to be greater in coverage, and
perhaps more organized given the forcing and shear profiles. So
we could see a somewhat greater damaging wind threat if any
organized linear structures materialize. However, low level
lapse rates will be poor and there's a notable lack of mid level
dry air to strengthen downdrafts. Overall, looking at marginal
risks of flash flooding and damaging wind gusts with greater
coverage and organization of storms anticipated on Friday.

Details for Saturday's convection remain unclear, but we could
certainly end up with some potential for flash flooding and severe
storms again. Current indications in the guidance support a
later timing of storms during the evening or even overnight
depending on the timing of a weak cold front and shortwave
trough.

We look to have a weak cold frontal passage by early Sunday, 
ushering in slightly drier air. This combined with subtle 
subsidence aloft will help briefly limit convection potential on
Sunday and also give some slight reprieve from the excessive
humidity, though highs will still be in the upper 80s to low 90s.
